pharm: Non-absorbed cation-exchange resin that, in the gastrointestinal tract (mainly the colon), exchanges sodium or calcium for potassium, binding potassium and removing it in the stool to lower elevated serum potassium.
quick: Oral: 15 g 1-4 times daily; rectal: 30-50 g as retention enema every ~6 h
Oral: mix powder in water (not fruit juice/food high in K+); separate from other oral drugs
Use if clearly needed; not absorbed (calcium form preferred)
Used in renal failure-related hyperkalemia; watch sodium/calcium and fluid
Serum potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium; bowel function (obstruction/necrosis)
summary: Polystyrene sulfonate is a non-absorbed cation-exchange resin used to treat hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium). It is available as the sodium salt (sodium polystyrene sulfonate, SPS) or the calcium salt (calcium polystyrene sulfonate). As the resin passes through the gut, predominantly the colon, it releases its sodium or calcium and binds potassium ions, which are then excreted in the feces, thereby lowering serum potassium. Its onset is slow (hours), so it is not appropriate as sole or initial therapy for life-threatening hyperkalemia, where rapid measures (calcium, insulin/glucose, beta-agonists, dialysis) are required. It is given orally or as a retention enema. Important safety concerns include serious gastrointestinal adverse events - intestinal necrosis, ulceration, and perforation - particularly when given with sorbitol, in postoperative patients, and in those with bowel dysfunction; for this reason concomitant sorbitol is no longer recommended. It can cause electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia) and, with the sodium form, sodium overload that may worsen heart failure or hypertension. Oral resin can bind other medications, so dosing should be separated from other oral drugs.
indications: Treatment of hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium), including in patients with chronic kidney disease or acute renal failure
Management of non-emergency hyperkalemia as an adjunct to dietary potassium restriction and treatment of the underlying cause

moa: Polystyrene sulfonate is a high-molecular-weight, non-absorbable cation-exchange resin in which sulfonate groups are loaded with sodium (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) or calcium (calcium polystyrene sulfonate). As the resin transits the gastrointestinal tract - predominantly in the large intestine, where potassium concentration is relatively high - the bound sodium or calcium ions are released in exchange for potassium ions, which become bound to the resin. The potassium-laden resin is then eliminated in the feces, removing potassium from the body and lowering serum potassium concentration. Because the exchange is not fully selective for potassium, the resin can also bind other cations such as calcium and magnesium, contributing to electrolyte disturbances. The process is gradual, accounting for the slow onset of the potassium-lowering effect.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to polystyrene sulfonate resins
Neonates with reduced gut motility (postoperative or drug-induced) - and oral administration in neonates
relative: Postoperative patients and those with conditions predisposing to impaired bowel motility (risk of intestinal necrosis)
Severe heart failure, hypertension, or marked edema (sodium form - sodium load)
Conditions predisposing to constipation or reduced GI transit
Patients requiring multiple concomitant oral medications (binding interactions)
monitor: Fluid status and signs of fluid overload (with the sodium form)
Bowel function - constipation, abdominal pain, distension (intestinal necrosis/obstruction)

preg: Polystyrene sulfonate is not absorbed systemically and may be used during pregnancy when treatment of hyperkalemia is needed; the calcium form is often preferred to avoid a sodium load. Use with attention to maternal electrolyte and fluid balance.
lact: The resin is not absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and is not expected to be present in breast milk, so it is considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Polystyrene sulfonate is commonly used to manage hyperkalemia associated with renal failure. There is no resin dose adjustment per se, but monitor closely: the sodium form adds a sodium load (problematic in oliguric/fluid-overloaded patients), and electrolyte shifts (potassium, calcium, magnesium) should be tracked. It is not a substitute for dialysis in severe cases.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is required, as the resin is not absorbed or metabolized. Standard monitoring of electrolytes applies.

major: Sorbitol (oral or rectal) - concurrent use is associated with intestinal necrosis; do NOT co-administer

Other oral medications - the resin binds many drugs (e.g., levothyroxine, lithium, digoxin, some antibiotics), reducing their absorption; separate dosing by at least 3 hours (6 hours in gastroparesis)
moderate: Cation-donating antacids and laxatives (e.g., magnesium hydroxide, aluminum/calcium-containing) - can cause systemic alkalosis and reduce the resin's potassium binding; avoid concurrent use
Digitalis glycosides - resulting hypokalemia increases the risk of digitalis toxicity
Diuretics and other agents affecting electrolytes - additive electrolyte disturbances
minor: Calcium and magnesium supplements - resin may bind these cations
interactions.food: Mix oral resin in water or a low-potassium vehicle; avoid potassium-rich juices and limit dietary potassium during therapy.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction with alcohol is described.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum potassium, sodium, calcium, and magnesium; the resin can lower these and the sodium form raises sodium - interpret electrolyte panels in this context.

serious: Fluid overload and worsening heart failure/hypertension (sodium form)
rare: Acute bronchitis/bronchopneumonia from inhalation of resin particles
emergency: Severe abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, rectal bleeding, or no passage of stool/gas (intestinal necrosis or obstruction)
Muscle weakness, palpitations, or fainting from severe potassium/electrolyte disturbance

monitoring: Serum potassium frequently to guide dosing and avoid overcorrection (hypokalemia)
Serum sodium, calcium, and magnesium during therapy
Fluid status, body weight, and signs of overload, especially with the sodium salt and in heart/renal failure
Bowel function - watch for constipation, abdominal distension, pain, or bleeding (intestinal necrosis/obstruction)
ECG in significant hyperkalemia or where electrolyte shifts may affect cardiac conduction
counsel: This medicine lowers high potassium by trapping it in your gut so it leaves in your stool; it works slowly and is not for a sudden emergency
Take the oral form mixed in water as directed - do not mix it with fruit juices high in potassium, and do not take it dry
Take your other medicines at least a few hours apart from this resin, because it can stop them being absorbed
Tell your team about constipation, and report severe stomach pain, swelling, vomiting, or any rectal bleeding right away
Report muscle weakness, palpitations, or feeling faint, which can signal an electrolyte problem
If you take the sodium form, watch for ankle swelling or breathlessness, especially if you have heart or kidney problems
pk: Potassium-lowering effect is slow, generally over hours (not minutes)

Not applicable - the resin is not absorbed systemically

pearls: Slow onset (hours) - NOT a treatment for acute, life-threatening hyperkalemia; use rapid measures first (IV calcium for cardiac protection, insulin/glucose, beta-agonists, dialysis) and use the resin for ongoing potassium removal

Do NOT give with sorbitol - the combination is linked to intestinal necrosis; serious GI events (necrosis, ulceration, perforation) are the most important safety concern, especially postoperatively and with bowel dysmotility

Sodium form delivers a significant sodium load - avoid or use cautiously in heart failure, hypertension, edema, and oliguria; the calcium form avoids the sodium load (but can cause hypercalcemia/binds magnesium)
The resin binds many oral drugs (levothyroxine, lithium, digoxin, others) - separate dosing by at least 3 hours (6 hours in gastroparesis)
Monitor potassium closely to avoid overcorrection, and watch calcium and magnesium; avoid cation-donating antacids/laxatives that can cause alkalosis and reduce efficacy
Roughly 1 g of resin exchanges about 1 mEq of potassium in vivo (variable); follow serum potassium rather than relying on fixed assumptions
missed: If a scheduled dose of polystyrene sulfonate is missed, take it when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose - do not double up. Because dosing is guided by serum potassium levels, follow your clinician's instructions and laboratory monitoring rather than self-adjusting.
overdose: Overdose or overtreatment leads to electrolyte disturbances, chiefly hypokalemia (causing muscle weakness, irritability, paralysis, ECG changes, and arrhythmias), and may cause hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, as well as gastrointestinal effects including fecal impaction or obstruction. Management is supportive: stop the resin, correct the electrolyte abnormalities (replace potassium, calcium, magnesium as needed), monitor the ECG, and manage any bowel complications.
